name: Kingdom of Loango
info: A Kongo-speaking kingdom of the Vili on the Atlantic coast north of Kongo, founded by Njimbe about 1565, remembered for its cloth and copper exports, its rotating succession and its merchants' slave trade.

facts.capital: Buali, in the province of Piri
facts.founder: Njimbe (Battel's "Gembe" or "Gymbe"), who very likely took the throne around 1565
facts.predecessor: Small coastal polities including Mayumba, Kilongo, Piri and Wansi; the founder came from Nzari in Kakongo, a vassal of the Kingdom of Kongo
facts.successor: European colonial rule in the 1800s (the Loango coast divided between what are now the Republic of the Congo, Gabon and Cabinda)

t: Njimbe's constitution rotated the throne among the rulers of four provinces, Kaye, Boke, Selage and Kabango, the ruler of Kaye succeeding when the king died.

Loango exported considerable copper to the European market and thousands of metres of cloth to Portuguese Luanda in the early seventeenth century; from the late seventeenth century its Vili merchants also traded in slaves on a considerable scale.
After King Buatu died in 1787 no king was elected for over a hundred years; a priest called the Nganga Mvumbi, who guarded the unburied body of the dead king, kept what remained of royal authority.
dyk: European ships never built permanent factories at Loango: they anchored offshore and dealt with royal officials called mafouks, who managed trade in the king's interest and kept direct European influence at arm's length.
ev: Sebastião de Souto, a priest in Kongo, records that King Diogo I has sent missionaries to convert Loango: the earliest documentary mention of the kingdom.
Njimbe, very likely the founder and first ruler of the traditions, takes the throne and reigns for 60 years, according to a Dutch description of 1625.
The English traveller Andrew Battel visits Loango and names Gembe, or Njimbe, as the predecessor of the reigning king.
Olfert Dapper's Dutch informants describe the government, religion and founding traditions of Loango, the only comprehensive account of the seventeenth century.
The Capuchin Bernardo Ungaro baptises the king as Afonso, and 6,000 of his subjects with him; a civil war between Christian and non-Christian parties follows his death.
Queen Verónica I of Ndongo-Matamba promises by treaty to stop trading with the Vili merchants operating in the Mbundu-speaking regions of eastern Angola.
French missionaries under Abbé Liévin-Bonaventure Proyart find a king who came to power only after a seven-year interregnum managed by a regent, the Mani Boman.
King Buatu dies and no successor is elected for over a hundred years; the Nganga Mvumbi holds residual royal authority.

sections.foundation:
The Kingdom of Loango was created by Kongo people on the Atlantic coast north of the more powerful Kingdom of Kongo, in what is now the western Republic of the Congo, southern Gabon and Cabinda. Its origins are obscure: the oldest complex society in the region was at Madingo Kayes, settled by the first century CE, but the archaeology says little more before the sixteenth century. Loango is absent from the titles of King Afonso I of Kongo in 1535. The earliest documentary reference is a mention around 1561 by Sebastião de Souto, a priest in Kongo, that King Diogo I (1545–61) had sent missionaries to convert Loango; in 1585 Duarte Lopes, Kongo's ambassador to Rome, called it a friend of Kongo and a former vassal.

Dutch visitors of the 1630s or 1640s recorded the first traditional account of its origin, reported by Olfert Dapper. The region had held small polities, Mayumba, Kilongo, Piri and Wansi among them, at war with each other. The founder, from Nzari in Kakongo, a vassal of Kongo, defeated his rivals through skilful alliances and built his capital at Buali in the province of Piri, from which the name Muvili derived. Andrew Battel, there about 1610, named the previous king as Gembe (Njimbe), and a Dutch description of 1625 said a ruler dead before that date had reigned 60 years from about 1565, so Njimbe was very likely the founder. The people, Bakongo speaking a northern dialect of Kikongo, included the Vili, the Yombe, Kunyi, Lumbu and Babongo Pygmies.
sections.socioeconomy:
Loango's wealth came from trade. In the seventeenth century Vili merchants travelled far in search of commercial opportunities, among the earliest to the copper mines of Mindouli and the territory of Bukkameale, perhaps the Niari valley; early Dutch records show Loango exporting considerable copper to the European market. The kingdom was also a major producer and exporter of cloth, to the interior and to the Portuguese at Luanda, where thousands of metres of Loango cloth were imported in the early seventeenth century. Free people paid taxes on their persons, land, slaves and livestock, collected by royal officials who sometimes overcharged.

From the late seventeenth century the Vili also engaged in the slave trade. Loango exported few slaves at first, but eventually did so in considerable quantities; some were acquired locally, many more from the interior. An early trade led to the Kingdom of Kongo, whose merchants sold slaves to Dutch and English shippers to avoid the taxes of Portuguese Luanda, and Vili communities were reported in São Salvador in 1656. By 1683 they operated in eastern Angola, and Portuguese efforts to stop them failed; the Vili also took up smithing. Their trade reached the Teke Kingdom and the Congo River beyond, and by the late eighteenth century slaves from the Bobangi area were a significant share of exports. European shippers built no factories: they anchored offshore and dealt with the mafouks, who managed trade in the royal interest.
sections.military:
Loango was made by war and alliance. In the founding tradition recorded by Dapper, the small polities of the coast each had their own leader and made war on each other; the founder from Kakongo triumphed through the skilful use of alliances, defeating those who opposed him, particularly Wansa, Kilongo and Piri, the last two of which required two wars to subdue. Once this was done, more northern regions, including Docke and Sette, submitted voluntarily, and the new king moved north to found settlements and his capital. At its height in the seventeenth century Loango's influence extended from Cape St Catherine in the north to almost the mouth of the Congo River.

The kingdom's later wars were largely its own. In 1663 the king was baptised as Afonso by the Capuchin Bernardo Ungaro, against considerable opposition; when he died a non-Christian took over, who was himself overthrown by one of the Christian party in 1665. This civil war was still going on in the 1670s, and the Christian party was in the end defeated, some of its members fleeing abroad, where one, Miguel da Silva, was elected ruler of Ngoyo and reigned there in 1682. Command of the army lay with the Makaka, the royal council's minister of war. Loango kept European power at a distance without fighting it: no shipper established a permanent factory on its coast. Many of the slaves its merchants sold were acquired in the interior rather than taken by Loango's own forces.
sections.governance:
In theory the kings of Loango held absolute and even divine power. Njimbe created a rule of succession in place around 1600: the king gave command of four provinces, Kaye, Boke, Selage and Kabango, to members of his family, and the throne rotated among them. When the king died the ruler of Kaye took over, as happened before 1624; the ruler of Boke took his place and the others advanced. By Dapper's description of about 1640 the king ruled closely over a cluster of villages around Loangogiri, each under a noble he appointed; outlying districts such as Mayumba followed their own rules under nobles sent from court, while Gobby had no royal supervision.

In 1701 the English merchant Nathaniel Uring found the king dead and power in the hands of the Mucundy, the Queen or Chief Governess, who oversaw women's affairs. By 1766, when Proyart's French missionaries arrived, there was no clear succession: anyone born of a princess could aspire to the throne, and the reigning king had taken power after a seven-year interregnum run by a regent, the Mani Boman. The electors, office-holders appointed by the dead king, chose the next. The council had offices: Magovo and Mapouto for foreign affairs, Makaka for war, Mfouka for commerce and Makimba, grand master of waters and forests. The king spent much time hearing cases. The people worshipped Nzambi a Mpungu and many nkisi served by nganga; Christian missions came repeatedly, but no permanent state church took root as in Kongo.
sections.impact:
Loango's reach was commercial. Its cloth clothed the interior and the Portuguese colony at Luanda, its copper went to Europe, and the Vili diaspora carried its traders across west-central Africa: into Kongo, where some converted to Christianity at São Salvador, into Ndongo-Matamba, where Queen Verónica I bound herself by treaty in 1683 not to deal with them, and inland to the Teke Kingdom and the Congo River. From the late seventeenth century that network fed the Atlantic slave trade through Dutch and English shippers off the Loango coast, with people from as far as the Bobangi country among those sold by the late eighteenth century.

The kingdom's engagement with Christianity began almost with its independence, when Diogo I of Kongo sent missionaries; Carmelites in 1583 and Jesuits in 1603 and 1628 reported conversions, and the Capuchin baptism of 1663 brought in 6,000 subjects before civil war defeated the Christian party. A black Jewish community on the coast, without links to Jews elsewhere, drew the interest of Enlightenment race scientists and of the German Loango Expedition of 1873–76. The constitution itself was remade by trade: Phyllis Martin argues that external commerce, especially the slave trade, enriched some nobles ahead of others, and that councillors who owed their positions to it came to dominate the king through ever longer interregna. The name Vili, attested from the seventeenth century as Mobili, remains that of the people today.
sections.decline:
The kingdom did not fall to an enemy; its monarchy wore away from within. In theory the king named his successor and placed him as ruler of Kaye, but by the eighteenth century there was so much contention over the position that kings died without naming a Ma-Kaye, and the electors took longer and longer to agree. The king who reigned in 1766 had waited seven years for his throne while the Mani Boman governed. Martin reads this as the work of a council enriched by the slave trade and strong enough to force the interregna out. After King Buatu died in 1787 no king was elected at all for more than a hundred years. Royal authority passed in part to the Nganga Mvumbi, the priest of the corpse, who oversaw the body of the dead king awaiting burial; several succeeded one another through the late eighteenth and nineteenth centuries.

Loango was still seeking Christianity in 1773 when French missionaries came, but the state ceased to exist during the European colonisation of Africa in the 1800s, when its lands were divided among the possessions that became the Republic of the Congo, Gabon and Cabinda. Missionaries on the coast at the end of the nineteenth century called its people Bafiote and their language Fiote; the traditions R. E. Dennett collected around 1890 still named Njimbe as the first king. What survived was the Vili people themselves, their Kikongo speech and their clans, and the memory of a kingdom whose kings had been chosen in turn from four provinces.

summary: The Kingdom of Loango, a Kongo-speaking state of the Vili founded about 1565 on the Atlantic coast north of Kongo, grew rich on cloth, copper and, from the late seventeenth century, the slave trade. Its rotating succession broke down under a council enriched by that trade, and after 1787 no king was elected before European colonisation ended it.
references: Phyllis Martin, The External Trade of the Loango Coast, 1576-1870: The Effects of Changing Commercial Relations on the Vili Kingdom of Loango (Oxford University Press, 1972)
Annie Mertet, Autour du Loango (XIVe-XIXe siècle): histoire des peuples du Sud-Ouest du Gabon au temps du royaume de Loango et du Congo français (Centre Culturel Français de Libreville, 1991)

pointDescs.1550: The register's starting point: the coastal polities of Mayumba, Kilongo, Piri and Wansi still war on one another, and Loango is not yet named in any document.
pointDescs.1561: Around this year Sebastião de Souto records that Diogo I of Kongo has sent missionaries to convert Loango, the earliest documentary mention of the kingdom.
pointDescs.1565: Njimbe, the founder of tradition, takes the throne about this year and reigns some 60 years, according to a Dutch description of 1625.
pointDescs.1585: Duarte Lopes, Kongo's ambassador in Rome, reports Loango as a friend of the King of Congo, said to have been a vassal in past times.
pointDescs.1610: Andrew Battel visits and names Njimbe as the previous king; Loango cloth is reaching Luanda by the thousands of metres and copper is going to Europe.
pointDescs.1625: A Dutch description records the death of the long-reigning king; the ruler of Kaye has succeeded under Njimbe's rotation of the four provinces.
pointDescs.1640: Dapper's informants describe a kingdom at its height, its influence reaching from Cape St Catherine to almost the mouth of the Congo, with provincial governors and a central district closely ruled from Loangogiri.
pointDescs.1663: The king is baptised Afonso with 6,000 of his subjects; opposition inside the country is considerable.
pointDescs.1665: The Christian party overthrows the non-Christian successor; the civil war that follows is still being fought in the 1670s.
pointDescs.1683: Vili merchants are trading in eastern Angola, where Queen Verónica I of Ndongo-Matamba promises by treaty to stop dealing with them; the slave trade grows.
pointDescs.1701: Nathaniel Uring finds the king dead and the Mucundy, the Chief Governess, governing the country.
pointDescs.1766: Proyart's missionaries find no clear rule of succession and a king who waited seven years in an interregnum run by the Mani Boman.
pointDescs.1787: King Buatu dies; no king is elected for over a hundred years, and the Nganga Mvumbi keeps what remains of royal authority.
pointDescs.1873: The German Loango Expedition of 1873–76 describes the coast; the kingdom survives only in its priests of the corpse and its trading officials.
pointDescs.1883: The register's end: Loango ceases to exist in the European colonisation of the 1800s, its coast divided among the possessions that became the Republic of the Congo, Gabon and Cabinda.

notes: The register's end year 1883 is not in the article, which says only that Loango ceased to exist during the European colonisation of the 1800s and that no king was elected for over a hundred years after Buatu's death in 1787.

The register's start 1550 precedes the article's chronology: the first mention is c. 1561 and the founder Njimbe very likely took the throne c. 1565 (Phyllis Martin argues for a late fourteenth- or early fifteenth-century foundation).
The article cites only two works in its Sources list, so there are two references rather than three.

The military section is thin because the article gives almost nothing on armies or weapons: only the founding wars, the civil war of 1663–1670s, the Makaka as minister of war and the kingdom's extent at its height.
The article gives two forms of the Capuchin's name (Bernardo Ungaro, Italian; Padre Berdardino d'Ungheria, Hungarian): the first was used.
Wansi/Wansa: the article spells the polity both ways; both are kept as the article has them in the respective passages.
